_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine seed -- subpoena and deposition timing. Phase 8.
Every value read from primary source 2026-08-23 and quoted in the row.
THE PHASE'S PREMISE WAS WRONG, AND CHECKING IT IS THE MAIN RESULT. Phase 8
was scoped on the expectation that subpoena response windows would share the
designated-period shape built in Phase 6, because they are 'often set by the
issuing party'. Verified against the rule text in all five jurisdictions:
they do not. Not one subpoena rule in any of the five uses the
designated-period shape. The instruction was to verify rather than build on
the assumption, and the verification is what stopped a wrong capability from
being reused on rules it does not fit.
WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE IS FOUR DIFFERENT SHAPES, only one of which the
engine can already express:
1. CAP: EARLIER OF A COMPUTED PERIOD AND A DATE THE ISSUING PARTY CHOSE.
Fed. R. Civ. P. 45(d)(2)(B): objections due 'before the earlier of the
time specified for compliance or 14 days after the subpoena is served.'
Ohio Civ.R. 45(C)(3) says the same thing in different words: 'within
fourteen days after service of the subpoena or before the time specified
for compliance if such time is less than fourteen days after service.'
This is NOT designated_period -- there is no floor and no party-chosen
DAY COUNT to validate. It is a computed period capped by a supplied DATE.
NOT SEEDED. The engine has no cap shape, and building one was not part of
this phase's approved scope. Flagged for a decision rather than
improvised, the same way the designated-period shape was named in Phase 5
and built as its own scoped phase in Phase 6.
2. STANDARD, NOT QUANTITY -- and this one can never be computed at all.
Every general deposition-notice rule in all five jurisdictions requires
only 'reasonable notice in writing': Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(1), Ohio
Civ.R. 30(A), Ind. T.R. 30(B)(1), Mich. Ct. R. 2.306(B), Pa.R.C.P.
4007.1. Indiana T.R. 45 likewise requires a motion to quash be made
'promptly and in any event at or before the time specified in the
subpoena for compliance', and Mich. Ct. R. 2.506 lets a subpoenaed person
object 'before the designated time for appearance'.
These set a STANDARD, not a period. There is no number to compute and no
capability that could ever make one appear. This is a fifth distinct rule
shape in this engine's experience and the only one that is permanently
uncomputable rather than merely unbuilt. The engine refuses, which is the
correct and final answer for these rules -- not a gap awaiting a phase.
3. FIXED PERIOD FORWARD FROM SERVICE. Michigan alone provides these, and
only for entity-directed process. Seeded below.
4. MINIMUM LEAD TIME, COUNTED BACKWARD FROM A SCHEDULED EVENT -- 'at least
X days before'. Michigan, Indiana and Pennsylvania each have one. These
ARE real operative deadlines and are seeded: the computed date is the
LAST DAY on which the act may be done, which is exactly what a lead-time
minimum means for the party who must act. Same shape as Fed. R. Civ. P.
6(c)(1), already seeded in Phase 5, and they use the existing backward
machinery with no new capability.
A NOTE ON WHY 'AT LEAST X BEFORE' IS A DEADLINE WHILE 'NOT LESS THAN X
AFTER' IS A FLOOR. These sound symmetrical and are not. 'Serve the notice at
least 20 days before service of the subpoena' fixes the last day the acting
party may act -- a deadline they can miss. 'A period designated in the
request, not less than 28 days' fixes a constraint on what someone ELSE may
demand of you, and says nothing about your deadline until they have chosen.
The first is computable from the rule alone; the second is not. Both were
read as minimums and only one produces a date.
PENNSYLVANIA'S SUBPOENA RULE IS A DIFFERENT PROCEDURE ENTIRELY, not a
variant of the others. Pa.R.C.P. 4009.21 has no recipient-objection window
at all: the party seeking production must first give twenty days' notice to
EVERY OTHER PARTY of an intent to serve, during which those parties may
object, and only then may the subpoena be served. The deadline that exists
belongs to the serving party before service, not to the recipient after it.
Seeded as what it is rather than mapped onto the federal shape.
NOT SEEDED, disclosed on the standing standard: everything in categories 1
and 2 above; state appellate deadlines and statutes of limitation, both
still explicitly out of scope.

rules.label: Last day to serve notice of an organizational deposition (Michigan — counted back from the deposition)

authority.quote: The notice shall be served at least 14 days prior to the scheduled deposition.
authority.note: BACKWARD-counted, and the only deposition-notice rule in any of the five jurisdictions with a day count -- general deposition notice everywhere requires only 'reasonable notice', which is a standard rather than a period and cannot be computed. The computed date is the LAST day the notice may be served. Under Mich. Ct. R. 1.108(1) the last day rolls, and for a backward period it rolls BACKWARD, so a 14th-day landing on a weekend or court holiday moves to the preceding business day — rolling forward would leave fewer than the 14 days the rule requires.

rules.label: Objections by an organization served with a deposition notice (Michigan)

authority.quote: No later than 10 days after being served with the notice, the noticed entity may serve objections or file a motion for protective order
authority.note: A FIXED forward period, and one of only two in this file. Ten days is short enough that Mich. Ct. R. 1.108 matters: Michigan has NO short-period exclusion, so intermediate weekends and holidays are counted and only the last day rolls — unlike Ohio and Indiana, whose rules would exclude them under seven days. Distinct trigger from the subpoena-directed 10-day rule in MCR 2.305(A)(6): one runs from a deposition NOTICE, the other from a SUBPOENA, and the engine must never guess which document was served.

rules.label: Objections by a non-party organization subpoenaed for a deposition (Michigan)

authority.quote: No later than 10 days after being served with the subpoena, the subpoenaed entity may serve objections, or file a motion for protective order
authority.note: SCOPE IS NARROW AND STATED HERE BECAUSE IT MATTERS: this applies to a subpoena naming a non-party ORGANIZATION for deposition purposes. It is not Michigan's general subpoena-objection rule — Mich. Ct. R. 2.506 lets a subpoenaed person object 'before the designated time for appearance', which sets no period and is not computable. A user with an ordinary document subpoena should not reach for this rule.

rules.label: Last day to serve a subpoena requesting documents (Michigan — counted back from the appearance)

authority.quote: Unless the court orders otherwise, the subpoena must be served at least 2 days before the appearance or 14 days before the appearance when documents are requested.
authority.note: Whether documents are requested changes the lead time from 2 days to 14, which is a fact about the subpoena the engine has no field for -- so the two are separate rules with separate triggers rather than one rule the engine would have to guess about. Same treatment as MCR 2.108(A)'s 21/28 split. Expressly displaced by a court order, quoted above.

rules.label: Last day to serve a subpoena not requesting documents (Michigan — counted back from the appearance)

authority.quote: the subpoena must be served at least 2 days before the appearance
authority.note: The shortest period anywhere in this engine, and a case where Michigan's lack of a short-period exclusion is decisive: two days counted backward includes intermediate weekends and holidays, and only the landing day rolls. Under Ohio's or Indiana's rules the same two days would exclude them and land materially earlier — which is why the computation standard is per jurisdiction and never shared by resemblance.

rules.label: Last day to confer before an organizational deposition (Indiana — counted back from the deposition)

authority.quote: At least fifteen days before the date of the deposition, the serving party and the organization or its counsel must confer in good faith about the matters for examination.
authority.note: A conferral deadline rather than a filing deadline, and a real one -- the obligation is mutual and the date is the last day it may be satisfied. Indiana's general deposition notice, like every other jurisdiction's, requires only 'reasonable notice' and is not computable; this fifteen-day conferral is the only computable deposition timing Indiana provides. Backward-counted under indiana_tr_6a: fifteen is above the seven-day threshold, so intermediate weekends and holidays are counted and only the last day rolls, backward.

rules.label: Last day to give other parties notice of intent to subpoena a non-party (Pennsylvania — counted back from the intended service)

authority.quote: A party seeking production from a person not a party to the action shall give written notice to every other party of the intent to serve a subpoena at least twenty days before the date of service.
authority.note: PENNSYLVANIA'S SUBPOENA PROCEDURE IS NOT A VARIANT OF THE OTHERS AND IS SEEDED AS WHAT IT IS. There is no recipient-objection window here at all: notice goes to every OTHER PARTY, not to the person named in the subpoena (4009.21(b) says so expressly), those parties may object during the twenty days, and only if none object may the subpoena be served. So the deadline that exists belongs to the SERVING party BEFORE service, not to the recipient after it. Counted backward from the intended service date; the computed date is the last day the notice may be given.
